reminder - consciousness might not have to run at human clock speeds. It could run much slower (or faster). Maybe the solar system is conscious somehow as it is "manipulating" bits somehow.
Do you think any special architecture is required for whatever consciousness is? That is, we are conscious but could a computer be conscious?
I feel like consciousness is simply pattern recognition. You are you because your pattern of atoms is unique.

I got a feeling that our brain is interacting with matter/energy, you can call it ether, that is outside our universe/dimension but this ether can be manipulated through means, like our brain, that we cannot understand yet. Our consciousness is maybe made up of this ether that exists outside our dimension. Just a wild hunch.

if humans reproduce more humans out of dirt then i guess so, assuming the body doesn't operate with the use of other forms of energy, otherwise, we'd have to consider the seemingly infinite and incomprehensible. A computer could recreate a map of energy beyond our senses, that we could interpret, but knowing whether or not they are or could be conscious would rely on that energy itself, I guess matter itself isn't enough.

Consider: you are composed of inert materials: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, potassium, etc., tec.. Individually none of these components is what we would call "alive". Amino acids, nucleic acids, proteins, and carbohydrates are all composed of these materials. Nothing special, shits all over the place. These chemicals can come together to form a self-replicating machine we call the living cell. In multi-cellular life, these self-replicating machines have developed the additional trick of self-organizing into a larger coherent whole. Everything beyond that is a matter of scales: complexity, number of cells and resources dedicated to a specific structure, etc..

There are projects that are actively unlocking the secrets of how the chemistry of biology works, starting with a single cell up to emulating entire organisms; to the best of my knowledge, the virtual flatworm, Openworm is the most advanced of the currently running projects open to public participation. Consider this: it is emulating an entire flatworm at the cellular level. The cell functions themselves are abstracted, but the networks between the various tissue cells, including neuronal cells, is emulated as closely as possible to the real organism. The input to this virtual creature is manipulated and compared to the response of similar inputs done on an actual flatworm. From my layman perspective, the model results are getting pretty damned close to the real thing. At what point do you need to consider that a computer is perfectly emulating the limited awareness of an unassuming flatworm?

So, what's the difference between a flatworm and a human? From a complexity perspective, a hell of a lot. From basic individual component hardware, not really all that much! It's mostly a matter of scale, and only a matter of time before a more complex life form can be emulated like this: say, a fish, a lizard, a mouse, maybe a small primate; eventually a human.

What I'm saying is: yes, hypothetically we have found nothing saying a consciousness cannot exist on other hardware than the animal brain. At this time, it looks like consciousness is more an emergent property related to system and behavioral complexity more than anything inherent to our being, so it could emerge from any number of complex, self-organizing systems. We're a very long way off still, but there's nothing in our understanding that would prevent a sufficiently complex network of computers from attaining consciousness. Probably not an individual CPU, no more so than a single cell could.

Additionally, as nano-tech develops and the lines continue to blur between what is alive and what is an artificial construct, we may find the answer of what is thought, what is the self; neurons are themselves tiny, naturally occurring machines just like any other cell.

I did a 'psychology news summary' for a final paper this past semester. The piece I focused on was by Desmurget et. al which basically found the stimulation of a group of neurons led to the desire to make a motion. Further stimulation led to the subject believing they had made the motion even though no motion had taken place. At the same time, stimulation of a separate group of neurons caused motion (sometimes large) without the subject realizing (experiencing) this motion.

Essentially, desire and the intention to do something is the experience of neurons which are already firing. That and a couple other articles (which I can't remember off the top of my head at the moment) provide further evidence to the following conclusion: Consciousness (and will) is an emergent property of the system in operation.

Hence I believe it's entirely possible for a computer to become conscious. Not as it currently stands, and when it happens, the machine certainly won't think in the same way we do, but it should be possible. The only real difference is the circuitry material and how the network is connected (also the sensors to the outside world it contains which could be (read: probably is) very important).

You do need some kind of feedback loop to achieve qualia. (http://m.youtube.com/watch?v=jTWmTJALe1w) This probably only works with neural networks with tangled connections. Which can be modelled by any Turing complete computer. But you never know, the brain might just be using some funky quantum effects which we don't know about yet.
